judgement.summary: A portfolio plan built on the snag list — the end-of-job defect document — repointed so that each thing Marta has touched is an item open until closed, carried by five numbered tags on string that scatter onto a map, turn to show what was wrong, unfold into each project's real material, and sort into Closed and Open with Calder Court's modelled-not-measured figure left swinging. Its greatest weakness is small invented texture in the tag copy — teaching "Tuesdays", Kirk Street "standing empty" then "occupied", the cabin "lived in", "a bare plot" — concrete-sounding details nothing in the material supports, sitting inside a plan that is otherwise scrupulous about attribution and permissions.

traps.evidence: "And is that the project's result or something you can point to as yours specifically?" (Q3); facts.md: "presumably firm's drawings she worked on. **See Q4.**"
"68% less heating demand than what, over what period — is that measured after the fact or modelled at design stage?"
"Your cv says 'Senior Architect, ARB.' LinkedIn shows 'Architect' (2020–2025) then 'Associate' ... What should the site call you?"
"Can these go on a personal site, and does he or the firm need crediting, or permission asking first?"
"What was your part in it specifically, who else worked on it, and are the boards yours to show or the firm's/team's?"

invented.claim: Teaching happens on Tuesdays — "second-years, Tuesdays, Clyde School" / "a studio, Tuesdays". The material says only "one day a week"; no day is named.
Kirk Street's church hall was "standing empty" before the conversion.
Kirk Street is now "occupied" and the cabin is "built and lived in" — occupancy outcomes stated as the grounds for marking both Closed.
invented.where: Third reply (chapter 6) and docs/story/storyboard.md, beat 6.1 caption

invented.claim: The cabin site was "a bare plot at Kashuby" — the plot's prior condition is nowhere in the material.

final.question: What's worth fixing, and how do you know it's fixed?
final.form: The snag list — the defect document carried on site at the end of a job, with the page's chapters named from it: Item 1 logged, Logged by, Location, Item, Action taken, Status, Sign-off
final.object: Five snag tags — numbered tabs on string — hanging off the plain outline of an ordinary building; they scatter onto a map, turn to show their faces, unfold into each project's exhibit, then sort into Closed and Open with one left swinging

swap.reason: The spine is particular to her — the 1:5 wall build-up she detailed, the cabin that is hers outright, and an ending that only reads honestly because her one headline figure is modelled with monitoring not yet begun.

backdrop.reason: The tags are the carrier of the content itself — their faces hold the facts, and in chapter 5 each unfolds into the wall section, the hall section, the timber frame, so deleting the 3D removes the exhibits, not decoration.

depth.reason: Seven chapters run in a consequential order — one tag logged, who logged it, where from, what was found wrong, what was done, what status it reached, sign-off — and the order cannot be shuffled.

clipart.reason: A snag tag is a working document from the trade rather than architecture's poster emblem (hard hat, blueprint, scale model), and it is on screen throughout.

honesty.reason: Calder Court is credited as the practice's project with a partner's concept and her as project architect, 68% is stated as modelled with monitoring this winter, the school is labelled a team of four, and the unpermissioned photos and drawings are carried as pending rather than faked.

thirty_seconds.reason: Beat 1.1 puts name, title, one line of what she does, the question and one proof figure on the unscrolled first screen, with a chapter rail and a skip-to-contact link visible from there.

plain_reader.reason: The opening is her name, "Associate, Field & Rowe Architects, Glasgow. Retrofit, timber, housing. ARB," a plain question and two figures — readable by a homeowner and not embarrassing to an architect, since the snag list is a real document rather than a borrowed metaphor.
